blocks.x: Collider's Steve Weintraub talks with Aaron Sorkin for The Social Reckoning.
Sorkin discusses how Facebook has evolved since The Social Network.
The writer-director also comments on legal notes and shaping key scenes in the edit.

Over a decade after Aaron Sorkin wrote The Social Network, the Oscar-winning writer-director returns with a companion feature, The Social Reckoning, about whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), the Facebook engineer who enlisted the help of a green Wall Street journalist, Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), to investigate the behemoth company’s questionable intentions.

In the movie, Haugen and Horwitz begin researching Facebook’s shift from a find-your-friends social media platform to a constant newsfeed fueled by an algorithm that churns contention, and the growing concerns and consequences of that evolution. The Social Reckoning also stars Oscar nominee Jeremy Strong (The Apprentice) as billionaire CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Academy Award nominee Wunmi Mosaku (Sinners) as Raya Akinola, Betty Gilpin (Widow’s Bay), Billy Magnussen (Violent Ends), and Bill Burr (Breaking Bad).

In this interview with Collider’s Steve Weintraub, Sorkin clarifies the connection between The Social Network and The Social Reckoning, discusses the “different realities” we’re fed through Facebook, and also comments on just how much legal interference he dealt with throughout the making of the movie. Check out all of this and more in the video above, with a transcript provided below.
Aaron Sorkin on Why There Won't Be Government Regulation of Big Tech
And how he dodged interference in his movie.

blocks.c: Aaron Sorkin on the set of The Social Reckoning with Mikey Madison.

blocks.x: COLLIDER: I'm doing a supercut right now, and the question is, where do you like to sit in a movie theater?
AARON SORKIN: You know what? For me, there isn't a bad seat in a movie theater. I don't even mind sitting in the front row. But I guess if I could pick any seat, it would be halfway up on an aisle.
SORKIN: Yeah. I don't know, I like the security of the aisle. But again, I'm happy sitting in any seat.

Thank you for indulging me on the question. Jumping into why I get to talk to you. Your film shines a very important light on Meta, who owns Facebook and Instagram. My big thing is, what do you think it's going to take for governments and our government to do anything to curb the misinformation that exists online, which your film brilliantly points out?

SORKIN: Listen, they can pass laws, but the problem is that there are about five tech oligarchs who are financing the campaigns of the people who pass laws, and that's why it's not going to happen, or that's why it hasn't happened.

It makes me so angry. I would imagine that when you're making something like this, you are possibly going to run into a wall where a lawyer says you cannot include this, so was there anything that you really wanted to include that lawyers were like, “Nope?”

SORKIN: No. Listen, under normal circumstances, there'd be a thorough legal vetting of a script of a nonfiction movie. In this case, they wouldn't hire an outside law firm just to concentrate on this film. There were notes, but nothing that hurt me. Changing somebody's name, that kind of thing. Little things, a few numbers, but nothing that hurt me. The lawyers, I'm happy to say, wanted us to make the film we wanted to make.
How Facebook Went From a Site for Friends to a World of "Different Realities"
"None of which, by the way, is being fact-checked."
If people sit down in the future and watch Social Network and Social Reckoning back to back, what do you hope the conversations are that they're having when the two films are over?

SORKIN: Well, first, let me say, I know there's been discussion about whether The Social Reckoning is a sequel, that kind of thing. It's another movie about Facebook, written by the same writer who wrote The Social Network, and one of the characters from The Social Network is in The Social Reckoning, sort of as if Henry Hill showed up in Casino.

If they watched the two movies back to back, I think the conversation would have to be about, “Well, wait… What changed? In 2010, it was this site where you kept track of your friends, and now it's something else.” Well, what changes is that they added the newsfeed. And once they added a newsfeed that was powered by an algorithm, it meant you were getting the news that you want while I was getting the news that I want, and she's getting the news she wants. We're all living in different realities — none of which, by the way, is being fact-checked.

I'm fascinated by the editing process because it's where it all comes together. You have these brilliant actors delivering these amazing takes. Talk a little bit about how the film was shaped in the editing room, possibly in a way you didn't expect. Did you end up with a lot of deleted scenes? I'm fascinated by the process.

SORKIN: Yeah, me too. Our editor, Alan Baumgarten, did a fantastic job with his post-production team. There isn't very much on the cutting room floor. A line here and there. I would say that certainly the climactic scene of the film, which I don't want to give away too much now, I knew that that was going to be something that was shaped in the editing. But we shot most of that on our first two days of shooting, and Alan would call me from the editing room saying, “It's going to work. It's going to work. This is cutting together. It's going to work.”
The Social Reckoning opens in theaters on October 9.
Stuart M. Besser, Todd Black, Aaron Sorkin, Peter Rice
